title: Network Theory Numericals 2: Resistor, Capacitor and Inductor

scenes.narration: Welcome back to the numericals series. Today we solve problems on the three basic components: reading a resistor's colour code with tolerance, the charge and energy of a capacitor, an RC timing problem, and the voltage across an inductor. These are short, scoring questions in every exam, so let's make sure you never lose marks on them.
scenes.title: R, C, L PROBLEMS
scenes.subtitle: Solved problems, step by step

scenes.title: Problem 1 · Colour code and tolerance
scenes.ask:
value, and the range of
the real resistance
scenes.narration: Problem one. A resistor has bands red, red, orange and gold. Find its value, and the range in which its real value can lie.

scenes.title: Problem 1 · Colour code and tolerance
scenes.narration: Step one. Red is two, and red again is two, giving twenty two. The third band, orange, is the multiplier, times one thousand. So the value is twenty two thousand ohms, twenty two kilo-ohms. The gold band means a tolerance of plus or minus five percent.

scenes.title: Problem 1 · Colour code and tolerance
scenes.narration: Step two, the range. Five percent of twenty two thousand is one thousand one hundred ohms. Subtract it for the minimum, twenty point nine kilo-ohms, and add it for the maximum, twenty three point one kilo-ohms. Any resistor reading between these values is within tolerance.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Charge and energy in a capacitor
scenes.narration: Problem two. A four hundred and seventy microfarad capacitor is charged to twelve volts. Find the charge stored and the energy stored.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Charge and energy in a capacitor
scenes.narration: Step one, convert to base units: four hundred and seventy microfarads is four hundred and seventy times ten to the minus six farads. Step two, the charge: Q equals C times V, which gives five point six four times ten to the minus three coulombs, five point six four millicoulombs.

scenes.title: Problem 2 · Charge and energy in a capacitor
steps: ! always convert µF to F first
scenes.narration: Step three, the energy: one half C V squared. Twelve squared is one hundred and forty four. Half times four seventy times ten to the minus six times one forty four gives about zero point zero three three eight joules, thirty three point eight millijoules. The commonest mistake is forgetting to convert microfarads into farads.

scenes.title: Problem 3 · RC timing
given: V = 9 V, R = 10 kΩ, C = 100 µF
scenes.ask:
τ, v_C after 2 s,
time to reach 5 V
scenes.narration: Problem three, a timing problem. A nine volt source charges an empty one hundred microfarad capacitor through a ten kilo-ohm resistor. Find the time constant, the capacitor voltage after two seconds, and the time it takes to reach five volts.

scenes.title: Problem 3 · RC timing
scenes.narration: Step one: tau equals R times C. Ten thousand ohms times one hundred times ten to the minus six farads gives exactly one second. Step two: the charging formula, v equals V times one minus e to the minus t over tau. At two seconds, e to the minus two is zero point one three five, so v is nine times zero point eight six five, about seven point seven eight volts.

scenes.title: Problem 3 · RC timing
scenes.narration: Step three: now we know the voltage and want the time. Set five equals nine times one minus e to the minus t. Divide by nine and rearrange: e to the minus t equals one minus five ninths, zero point four four four. Take the natural log of both sides: minus t equals minus zero point eight one one. So it takes about zero point eight one seconds to reach five volts. This rearranging with ln is a favourite exam step.

scenes.title: Problem 4 · Voltage across an inductor
scenes.narration: Problem four. The current in a fifty millihenry inductor rises steadily from zero to two amperes in ten milliseconds. Find the voltage across the inductor while the current rises, and the energy stored at the end.

scenes.title: Problem 4 · Voltage across an inductor
scenes.narration: Step one: the rate of change of current. Two amperes in ten milliseconds, which is zero point zero one seconds, gives two hundred amperes per second. Step two: V equals L times d i by d t. Zero point zero five henries times two hundred is ten volts.

scenes.title: Problem 4 · Voltage across an inductor
steps: ! mH → H and ms → s first
scenes.narration: Step three: the energy stored when the current reaches two amperes: one half L I squared, half times zero point zero five times four, zero point one joules. Remember to convert millihenries to henries and milliseconds to seconds before you calculate.

Exam tips for component problems. In the colour code, the first bands are digits and the next is the multiplier. Learn the prefixes: micro is ten to the minus six, milli ten to the minus three, kilo ten to the three. Remember the three energy and charge formulas. To find a time in an RC problem, rearrange and use the natural log. And for an inductor, the voltage depends on how fast the current changes.
